summary: Describes the NEA Asokan Attack, a subtle forwarding attack against Network Endpoint Assessment protocols, which check the health of devices joining a network. It explains how the attack works and what countermeasures can be used. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6813 explains an attack on the checks a network runs before it lets a device in. The attacker relays the check between two of their own machines, so that the machine the network finally examines appears healthy even though it is not. The RFC then shows how binding the check cryptographically to the secure connection that carried it stops the relay from working.

subtitle: How an attacker can make a sick computer look healthy to a network access check, and how to stop it.

tldr.problem: The protocols that check whether a device is healthy before it joins a network can be fooled. An attacker who controls a machine in the middle can make the check report on a different, clean device.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the attack step by step and then sets out two ways to stop it: binding the identities used when the secure tunnel was set up into the posture exchange, and cryptographically binding the posture exchange to that tunnel.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends that the tunnel-based posture transports use the same binding mechanism, and names the tls-unique channel binding value as the preferred way to do it.

today: RFC 6813 is an Informational RFC published in December 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents an attack on the NEA posture transport protocols and recommends that PT-TLS and PT-EAP use the same cryptographic binding mechanism.

sections.title: A Relay Attack Against Network Access Checks
sections.content:
The Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) protocols are subject to a subtle forwarding attack that has become known as the NEA Asokan Attack. This RFC describes the attack and the countermeasures that may be mounted against it. The posture transport protocols developed by the NEA working group, PT-TLS and PT-EAP, include mechanisms that can provide cryptographic-binding and identity-binding countermeasures.

NEA is built from nested protocols. The Posture Attribute (PA) protocol is nested inside the Posture Broker (PB) protocol, which is nested inside the Posture Transport (PT) protocol. Used together, they let an NEA Server assess the security posture of an endpoint, and the server may then decide whether to grant network access or use the information for other purposes.

The RFC is not a specification and it does not change any protocol. Its purpose is to show that the attack is real, to set out the defences that are available, and to say which of them the transport protocols should use. Its scope is narrow on purpose: the analysis covers this one attack, not every possible attack on NEA.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a device is let onto a network, the network can check that it is healthy. This RFC describes a way to cheat that check by relaying it between two machines the attacker controls, and then sets out the defences.

sections.title: How the Attack Works
sections.content:
The NEA Asokan Attack is a variation on an attack described in a 2002 paper by Asokan, Niemi and Nyberg. In the original attack, an authorized user is tricked into authenticating to a decoy Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) server. That decoy forwards the authentication protocol from one tunnel to another, so the real AAA server believes the messages originated from the attacker's machine and grants it access.

The NEA version of the attack works the same way with posture messages. The attacker wants to trick GoodServer into believing that DirtyEndpoint has good security posture, which could allow, for example, an infected machine onto a network where it could infect others. The attacker forwards PA messages from CleanEndpoint through BadServer to DirtyEndpoint, which sends them on to GoodServer. GoodServer is then tricked into thinking that the PA messages came from DirtyEndpoint, and therefore considers DirtyEndpoint to be clean.

Two things make the relay work. The posture messages carry no proof of which endpoint they came from, and the server has no way to tell that the exchange it is taking part in is the same one the endpoint is taking part in. Fixing either of those gaps breaks the attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The attacker owns two machines. A clean one answers the health check, and a dirty one forwards that answer to the server. The server believes the healthy answer came from the dirty machine and lets it in.

sections.title: Lying Endpoints and the Measurement Agent
sections.content:
There are simpler attacks against NEA than the Asokan attack, such as lying endpoint attacks, where an endpoint simply lies about its posture. That is easy to do, but there are defences against it. One is the External Measurement Agent (EMA): hardware, software or firmware that is especially secure, hard to compromise, and designed to report accurately on the configuration of the endpoint it lives in. It observes and reports on critical aspects of endpoint posture, such as which security-relevant firmware and software have been loaded.

When an EMA is used, the PA messages that reliably and securely establish the endpoint's posture are exchanged between the EMA itself and a Posture Validator on the NEA Server. The Posture Collector on the endpoint, and any other intermediaries between the EMA and the Posture Validator, are not trusted; they pass messages along as untrusted intermediaries.

To make sure the EMA's messages reach the validator accurately even if the collector or another intermediary has been compromised, those PA messages must provide integrity protection, replay protection and source authentication between the EMA and the Posture Validator. Confidentiality is not needed, at least with regard to the software on the endpoint, but the integrity protection should also cover message deletion and session truncation. Organisations that have built EMAs have typically also built remote attestation protocols with these properties, such as the Trusted Computing Group's Platform Trust Service protocol binding to IF-M. Detecting lying endpoints is out of scope for NEA, but the NEA protocols have to support the technologies that make it possible, which is why they must also support countermeasures against the Asokan attack.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can simply lie about its own health, so some setups put the health check inside a small trusted part of the device that is hard to tamper with. The RFC says that this trusted part must still prove where its answers really came from, or the relay attack works just as well.

sections.title: Two Ways to Bind the Answer to the Connection
sections.content:
The first countermeasure is identity binding. One way to mitigate the Asokan attack is to bind the identities used when the tunnel was set up into a cryptographic exchange at the PA layer. That goes a long way towards preventing the attack, but it does not bind the exchange to a specific TLS session, which is desirable. There is also no standard way to extract an identity from a TLS session, which could make implementation difficult.

The second countermeasure is cryptographic binding. The PA exchange is cryptographically bound to the PT exchange and to any keying material or privileges granted as a result of the two exchanges. This allows the NEA Server to be sure that the PA messages pertain to the same endpoint as the party that terminated the PT exchange, and that no other party gains any access or advantage from the exchange.

The two work at different levels. Identity binding says which names were used when the tunnel was created; cryptographic binding says that the posture conversation and the tunnel conversation are the same conversation. The RFC's conclusion favours the second, with the first as a possible addition, because the second is what actually prevents the messages from being carried from one endpoint to another.
sections.plainLanguage: Two defences are available. One mixes the names used when the secure connection was made into the health check. The other ties the health check to that exact secure connection, so a relayed answer no longer matches.

sections.title: Where the Binding Data Can Come From
sections.content:
Both PT-TLS and PT-EAP involve TLS, so the RFC concentrates on TLS-based solutions that work with either transport. The TLS handshake establishes a cryptographic state between the TLS client and the TLS server, and several mechanisms can export information derived from that state. The client and server each include that information in their own calculations, which binds the instance of the tunnel into the PA protocol.

Two export mechanisms are described. Keying material export, defined in RFC 5705, lets additional secret key material be extracted from the TLS master secret. The tls-unique channel binding value, defined in RFC 5929, is data extracted from the TLS handshake finished message, and RFC 5929 defines several quantities that can be extracted from a TLS session to bind that session to other protocols.

The choice of cipher suite matters. To eliminate the possibility of a man-in-the-middle attack, and to thwart the Asokan attack when the keying material export mechanism is used, neither TLS endpoint may be in sole control of the TLS pre-master secret. Cipher suites based on key transport, such as the RSA cipher suites, do not meet this requirement, so Diffie-Hellman cipher suites such as RSA-DHE are required. The same applies when key material extracted from the tunnel is used to derive ciphering keys in another protocol, as EAP-TLS does. Finally, the EMA needs to obtain the binding data from the TLS exchange and to prove knowledge of it in an exchange that has integrity protection, source authentication and replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The value that ties the two conversations together comes from the secure connection itself. The RFC compares two ways of extracting it, and warns that the connection must use a key agreement method in which neither side alone controls the secret, or the binding proves nothing.

sections.title: Conclusions and Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC makes three recommendations. Protocols should make use of cryptographic binding, and binding the identities of the tunnel endpoints in the EMA may also be useful. In particular, the layer 2 and layer 3 TLS-based posture transports, PT-TLS and PT-EAP, should use the same cryptographic binding mechanism. The preferred approach is to use the tls-unique channel binding value, which will be made available to the EMA that will use it. This approach can use any TLS cipher suite based on a strong cipher algorithm, because it does not depend on the keying material export mechanism.

On security, the RFC is explicit about its own limits. Analysing and proposing countermeasures for the NEA Asokan Attack does not mean it covers all the possible attacks against the NEA protocols or the NEA Reference Model. For a broader security analysis, the reader is pointed to the Security Considerations sections of the NEA Overview, PA-TNC, PB-TNC, PT-TLS and PT-EAP.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's advice is to tie the health check to the secure connection in one consistent way across the transport protocols, using a value taken from the TLS handshake. It also says plainly that it has analysed one attack, not all of them.
